marble.name: Estimating Lengths
marble.subject: Mathematics
marble.description: Estimate lengths by comparing with a known reference unit and check by measuring: informal units (e.g. paper clips, cubes, hand spans) at an early stage, and standard units (inches, feet, centimetres and metres, as in US Grade 2) when those units are known
marble.prompt: Before measuring something, can you make a sensible guess of how long it is — like 'about 8 paper clips' or 'about 30 centimetres' — and then measure to check how close they were?

cluster.summary: Your child is learning about measurement in everyday life — telling time to the hour and half-hour, comparing lengths and weights of objects, understanding money, and using time words like yesterday and tomorrow.

misconceptions: Wild guessing with no referent — numbers untethered to any known length, often off by an order of magnitude.
Unit/scale confusion — estimating a book at '20 m' rather than about20cm, muddling centimetres and metres. A300cm room length can be valid (3m), so equivalent sensible units are accepted.
Not committing before measuring — treats estimation as pointless and reaches straight for the ruler.
Never recalibrating — measures but doesn't compare with the estimate, so the mental ruler never improves.
representations: Personal benchmark referents calibrated by actual measurement: fingernail, hand-span, stride and doorway; no universal1m childstride
A 'mental ruler' / mental number line of length magnitudes
Everyday reference objects (an inch-long piece of gum, a metre stick)
authoredAnswer: The child gives a committed estimate in an appropriate unit BEFORE measuring, grounded in a referent or mental ruler ('the door is about 2 m — a bit taller than me'; 'my fingernail is about 1 cm so the book is around 20 cm'), lands in the right order of magnitude, then measures and judges how close, adjusting the next estimate.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Blurts an estimate with no basis ('a hundred?'), wildly off; when asked how, has no referent to name.
wrongAnswers.fix: Teach and rehearse checked personal benchmarks against an actual ruler/metre stick. Compare the learner's own finger width/stride with known units rather than assume a child's stride is1m; then mentally iterate a suitable reference and measure to check.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Estimate is a reasonable figure attached to the wrong-sized unit for the object.
wrongAnswers.fix: Use an actual1cm/1m reference and calibrate any personal benchmark against it. Sanity-check the estimate against the real object; accept equivalent sensible units such as300cm or3m for the same length.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Treats estimate and measurement as unrelated; no reflection on over/under; next estimate no better.
wrongAnswers.fix: Build the compare-and-revise habit — 'were you over or under? by how much? what will you change next time?' — across several objects.

before.name: Measuring length (age 6+)
before.reason: Basic prerequisite (Ontario G1 readiness review): Measuring length with same-size units is the real prerequisite.

before.name: Measuring length (age 7+)
before.reason: Softened (Ontario G1 readiness review): Core skill (estimate with a known unit, check by measuring) needs measuring with same-size units; the ruler/standard-tool branch stays explicitly supported in evidence and as a soft prerequisite.
